Read: 7400 MB/s Write: 6400 MB/s Endurance: 600 TBW Warranty: 5 years Interface: M.2 4.0 x 4 The refreshed Sabrent Rocket 4 1TB drops the DRAM, goes single-sided and keeps 7,400/6,400 MB/s Gen4 ratings — TweakTown ranked it among the best Gen4 drives. Controller & Memory The Sabrent Rocket 4 1TB carries a name that has been around since 2020, but the drive wearing it today is a different machine. The original paired Phison's E16 with DRAM and 96-layer TLC for 5,000/4,400 MB/s; the current revision — SKU SB-RKT4L, sold on Amazon as Rocket 4 DRAM-Less — is a clean-sheet refresh built on Phison's four-channel PS5027-E27T running DRAM-less with Host Memory Buffer, behind Kioxia BiCS6 TLC. The rated numbers moved forward anyway: 7,400 MB/s sequential reads and 6,400 MB/s writes over PCIe 4.0 x4, with 1,000K random-read and 950K random-write IOPS, all on a single-sided M.2 2280 board. It is, component for component, the same silicon Corsair uses in the MP600 Elite. Single-sided is the quiet headline. With every chip on one side, the drive fits the shallow slots of thin laptops, handhelds and the PS5 without modification, and Sabrent's low-power claims for the E27T platform make it a credible console and portable upgrade — Tom's Hardware's testing found it drawing less power than Crucial's T500, itself an efficiency benchmark in the Gen4 field. The competition frames the value question. Corsair's MP600 Elite shares the platform and usually undercuts on price; the WD Black SN850X and Samsung 990 Pro keep their DRAM caches and sit a tier above in sustained work; Crucial's T500 fights the same DRAM-less flagship fight. Sabrent's counter is a five-year warranty stated with no registration required — a break from the company's older practice — plus a verdict from TweakTown that placed this refresh among the best Gen4 drives currently available. TweakTown's 1 TB review measured 104 MB/s at 4K Q1T1 — the strongest low-queue random-read figure the outlet had recorded from a DRAM-less drive — and the platform's Phison-origin I/O+ and DirectStorage support put the drive among the Gen4 models best prepared for modern game-streaming features. Tom's Hardware's testing of the 2 TB sibling confirmed the efficiency story, with power draw beating the Crucial T500. In TweakTown's PS5 testing the drive read at 6,497 MB/s, comfortably above Sony's 5,500 MB/s recommendation. The DRAM-less trade appears exactly where expected: sustained writes. A pseudo-SLC cache absorbs bursts at full speed, and once it fills, throughput settles well below the 6,400 MB/s headline — TweakTown's post-cache charts were unflattering, as they are for every drive on this platform. For boot-and-games duty the cache rarely empties; for scratch-disk or backup workloads, a DRAM-equipped rival such as the SN850X holds its speed longer. Nothing about the ratings suggests more than the platform delivers, and the platform delivers at the top of the DRAM-less class. Sabrent Rocket 4 vs Competitors See how the Rocket 4 stacks up against other M.2 4.0 x 4 drives in our database: Compare with rival drives: ADATA XPG Gammix S70 Blade 1 TB Patriot Viper VP4300 1 TB Acer Predator GM7000 1 TB Endurance, TBW & Warranty Sabrent warrants the Rocket 4 1TB for five years, and the current product listing states explicitly that no registration is required — a welcome change from older Sabrent SSDs, which needed registration to unlock the full term. The endurance picture is less explicit: Sabrent's product pages leave TBW unpublished for this revision. Tom's Hardware's launch coverage of the refresh put the allocation at 600 TBW per 1 TB of capacity — 600 TBW at this size — and that figure is the best capacity-specific number available. At 20 GB of writes per day, 600 TBW stretches past 80 years, so the warranty term, not the flash, is the practical limit. The MTBF figure is unpublished, and claims run directly through Sabrent's US-based support, a channel with a generally responsive reputation among enthusiasts, subject to standard proof-of-purchase practice. The Sabrent Rocket 4 1TB is the pick for buyers who want top-of-class Gen4 speed in a single-sided, laptop-and-PS5-friendly package and can live with DRAM-less sustained behavior — TweakTown's ranking of it among the best Gen4 drives is consistent with both its silicon and its measured results. Skip it for heavy sustained writing, where the WD Black SN850X's DRAM cache holds its pace long after the Rocket 4's pseudo-SLC cache empties. Corsair's MP600 Elite pairs identical hardware and deserves a price comparison before committing. As the DRAM-less refresh of a legacy name, the Sabrent Rocket 4 1TB finally makes that name mean something again — with the usual Sabrent premium attached. + Pros 7,400/6,400 MB/s Gen4 ratings Single-sided PCB suits laptops and PS5 1,000K/950K rated random IOPS 5-year warranty, no registration needed Lower power draw than Crucial T500 104 MB/s 4K Q1T1 in TweakTown testing - Cons DRAM-less: HMB instead of onboard cache Sustained writes fall once the pSLC cache fills No TBW figure published by Sabrent No heatsink included 3 / 5 · 44 votes Buy this or similar SSD Storage: Samsung 980 Pro 2 TB -57% $165 List Price: $379.99 Buy on Amazon INLAND Performance Plus 1 TB $79.99 Buy on Amazon Silicon Power 512GB NVMe SSD $42.97 Buy on Amazon Video Review Mail Day: Sabrent 1tb Gen 4 NVME Frequently Asked Questions Is the Sabrent Rocket 4 1TB compatible with the PS5? Yes, subject to adding a heatsink. Sony recommends a PCIe 4.0 drive reading at least 5,500 MB/s with cooling attached, within dimensions of 110 x 25 x 11.25 mm. The Rocket 4 1TB rates 7,400 MB/s reads, its single-sided board fits the size limit easily, and TweakTown's PS5 testing measured 6,497 MB/s on the platform — well above the guidance. The drive ships bare, so budget for a low-profile PS5-compatible heatsink. One terabyte is also workable console capacity, though 2 TB suits larger libraries better. Is the Sabrent Rocket 4 1TB good for gaming? Yes — that is this revision's core audience. The 7,400 MB/s read rating is at the PCIe 4.0 ceiling, TweakTown measured 104 MB/s at 4K Q1T1, the best low-queue random-read result it had recorded from a DRAM-less drive, and the platform supports DirectStorage for games built on it. One terabyte holds an operating system plus a rotating library, and the drive's low power draw suits handhelds and small builds. Sustained-write weakness barely touches gaming, since installs are bursts; the DRAM-less design only shows in long, cache-busting transfers. Does the Sabrent Rocket 4 1TB have a DRAM cache? No — this is the biggest change from the original. The refreshed Rocket 4 (SKUs SB-RKT4L-1TB and SB-RKT4L-2TB) uses Phison's DRAM-less PS5027-E27T controller with Host Memory Buffer holding the translation tables in system RAM, paired with Kioxia BiCS6 TLC. The 2020 original used a DRAM-equipped E16 design; the Rocket 4 Plus line still carries DRAM on Phison's E18. Despite losing the cache, the refresh's rated speeds and measured low-queue random reads improved over the old drive — TweakTown's verdict placed it among the best Gen4 drives available. What is the TBW endurance of the Rocket 4 1TB? Sabrent's own product pages do not publish a TBW figure for this revision, which is unusual and worth knowing. The best capacity-specific data comes from Tom's Hardware's launch coverage of the refresh, which put the endurance allocation at 600 TBW per 1 TB of capacity — hence 600 TBW here, doubling to 1,200 TBW on the 2 TB model. For scale, at 20 GB of writes per day the 600 TBW budget lasts more than 80 years, so the five-year warranty is the practical limit. The original 2020 Rocket 4 carried a higher 1,800 TBW rating at 1 TB. Sabrent Rocket 4 or Rocket 4 Plus — what is the difference? They are different drives sharing a name. The current Rocket 4 (SB-RKT4L) is the 2024-refresh: Phison's DRAM-less E27T controller, Kioxia BiCS6 TLC, single-sided PCB, capacities of 1 TB and 2 TB, rated 7,400/6,400 MB/s. The Rocket 4 Plus is the older flagship: Phison's DRAM-equipped E18 controller, Micron 176-layer TLC, double-sided at higher capacities, a range stretching from 500 GB to 8 TB, and the line's highest endurance ratings. Choose the Plus for sustained-heavy work and capacities beyond 2 TB; choose the refreshed Rocket 4 for efficiency, laptops, the PS5 and lower price. Sabrent Rocket 4 1TB or Corsair MP600 Elite 1TB? They share the same platform — Phison's E27T controller and Kioxia BiCS6 TLC — so peak performance is effectively identical, and TweakTown's reviews treated them as inseparable on speed. The differences are packaging and brand terms: Corsair frequently prices the MP600 Elite lower and offers it in more retail channels, while Sabrent answers with its no-registration five-year warranty, US-based support and the single-sided, efficiency-tuned implementation Tom's Hardware highlighted. Since the silicon is the same, price should decide this comparison; whichever costs less on the day is the rational buy. Comments Be the first to comment. Comments are reviewed before they appear.
